about: Authored countries a generated world may hold, each where its requirements fit: beyond a march on the side named, of a country of one of the terrains named. The first march a company reaches where one fits leads into it instead of a country drawn from the seed; each is placed once in a world (src/world/frontier.ts). Of the countries among one kind (the independent adventures), the first region's marches lead into only the one its seed chooses; the rest lie further out, each beyond a country drawn from the seed (Countries.plan), so that a world holds them all. Each says what the folk of the first region say of it (rumour, with {keeper} whoever keeps travellers in the town it is asked in), what it is asked about (topic), what the company knows of it once told (heard), what is said of it a country further off (far: "where ..."), what is seen of it from somewhere high in the country next to it, over the march (skyline: the builder's, from what its folk say of it, for its authors to rewrite), and, for one whose news is posted, the notice every town of the first region has nailed up (notice); and, for one that says when it is seen through, how the talk goes there after and what whoever keeps travellers says to the company come back from it (after).

countries.name: Merrowdale
countries.topic: the forty crowns in Merrowdale
countries.rumour: 'Up the north road there is Merrowdale,' says {keeper}. 'There is a long ridge across the head of the dale, and they say a giant king is buried under it. Something tall walks the crest at night. The steward has posted forty crowns to have it laid.'
countries.heard: Up the north road lies Merrowdale, where a giant king is said to be buried under the long ridge, and something tall walks its crest at night.
countries.skyline: a long ridge laid straight across the head of a dale, too straight for a hill
countries.far: a giant king is buried under a long ridge, and something tall walks its crest at night

notice.name: a notice from Merrowdale
notice.text: A notice in a clerk's hand, carried down from Merrowdale and nailed up where travellers will see it: WHOEVER LAYS THE MOWER THAT WALKS THE LONG MAN SHALL HAVE FORTY CROWNS OF THE STEWARD. A. VENN, FOR THE LORD. Under it someone has written: up the north road, three days at most.
notice.talk: A notice from Merrowdale is nailed up where travellers will see it, and half the talk is of the forty crowns it offers and the other half of why nobody has gone.

after.talk: A notice from Merrowdale still hangs where travellers will see it, curling at the corners. Nobody talks of the forty crowns now: the word down the north road is that the Long Man is quiet.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, all of it, without a word. 'There was word of it already,' {keeper} says then. 'Off the north road: the thing on the ridge is quiet, and nobody up there talks of forty crowns any more. Nobody said who.' {keeper} looks at you a while longer, then reaches up and takes the notice from Merrowdale down, and puts it on the fire.

countries.name: Thrume
countries.topic: Saltgrave, in the east of the country
countries.rumour: 'Away in the east of the country, under the fells, there is a salt town, Saltgrave,' says {keeper}. 'People pay to sleep there, and some of them do not come home. And the giants have come down off the mountain, they say, for the first time anyone remembers.'
countries.heard: Away in the east of the country lies Saltgrave, a salt town under the fells, where people pay to sleep and some do not come home, and the giants have come down off the mountain.
countries.skyline: smoke going up from salt-pans under the fells
countries.far: people pay to sleep in a salt town under the fells, and some of them do not come home

after.talk: The talk of Saltgrave in the east has changed in the telling: the salt did not come for a week and then it did, and nobody who drinks it will say what is different.
after.told: {keeper} listens to all of it, the salt town and the sleeping houses and the giants in their hall, with one hand flat on the bar. 'There was a week the salt did not come up the road,' {keeper} says, 'and then there was salt again. I did not ask what had been done to it.' {keeper} pours a drink and slides it across, and does not pour one for the company's account. 'I'll thank you not to tell me while I'm serving.'

countries.name: the Strewnfield
countries.topic: the room of glass in the Strewnfield
countries.rumour: 'South, in the Strewnfield,' says {keeper}, 'a room of glass fell into a barley field by Cobble Ring. It grows, they say, wherever nobody is watching it. They sit up with it all night on stools.'
countries.heard: South of here lies the Strewnfield, where a room of glass fell into a barley field by Cobble Ring, and grows wherever nobody watches it.
countries.skyline: a flash in the fields, like a window where no house stands
countries.far: a room of glass fell into a barley field, and grows wherever nobody is watching it

countries.name: the Corrow
countries.topic: the mountain over the Corrow
countries.rumour: 'West of here is the Corrow,' says {keeper}. 'There is a mountain hangs over it in the sky, on a chain, and they say it is drifting. And there is a well there nobody has been to the bottom of.'
countries.heard: Away in the west of the country lies the Corrow, where a mountain hangs in the sky on a chain, drifting, over a well nobody has been to the bottom of.
countries.skyline: a mountain hanging in the sky, with nothing under it but air
countries.far: a mountain hangs in the sky on a chain, drifting, over a well nobody has been to the bottom of

countries.name: the Ghessil Uplands
countries.topic: the Ghessil Uplands
countries.rumour: 'West, up on the Ghessil Uplands,' says {keeper}, 'there is a light lies on the glass that slows whatever drinks it. There are people standing in it, they say, that went in last autumn and are standing there yet, alive.'
countries.heard: Away in the west of the country lie the Ghessil Uplands, where a light on the glass slows whatever drinks it, and people stand in it alive since last autumn.
countries.skyline: a light lying on the uplands that does not move when the clouds do
countries.far: a light lies on the glass that slows whatever drinks it, and people stand in it alive

countries.name: the Bowl of Ammerlin
countries.topic: the falling water at Ammerlin
countries.rumour: 'Away in the south of the country there's a city down the inside of a crater, Ammerlin,' says {keeper}. 'Their lake's been going down three years, and nobody there will believe anybody else about why. So they've sent out for someone from outside to measure it, and put their name to the answer. The Office of Measures pays, if you can count.'
countries.heard: Away in the south of the country lies the Bowl of Ammerlin, a city down the inside of a crater, whose lake has been falling for three years; its Office of Measures wants someone from outside to measure it and say why.
countries.skyline: the rim of a great crater, with smoke going up out of it
countries.far: a city down the inside of a crater is losing its lake, and nobody there believes anybody else about why

countries.name: the Ossel delta
countries.rumour: 'Down the east road, where the marsh meets the sea, there's Tessary on the Ossel,' says {keeper}. 'Their legions came home from the war a week back, and they say some of the soldiers are getting up in the night and walking into the sea. Barefoot, in step, eyes open. An eel-wife there has put up a notice: she'll give her savings to anyone who can tell her where her boy went.'
countries.heard: Away in the east of the country lies Tessary on the Ossel, where the legions have come home from the war and some of the soldiers walk into the sea at night; an eel-wife there offers her savings for news of her son.
countries.skyline: the smoke of a town where the marsh meets the sea
countries.far: the legions have come home from the war, and some of the soldiers walk into the sea at night

after.talk: The east road's news of Tessary has gone from soldiers walking into the sea to a quarrel about paper. Nobody can say who has the note, only that somebody does.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, the legions and the sea-walkers and the note, and is quiet while the lamp is trimmed. 'They stopped walking into the sea,' {keeper} says. 'That much came up the east road. The rest came as a quarrel about paper, and I never could follow a quarrel about paper.' {keeper} thinks. 'An eel-wife used to put up a notice about her boy. I am told it has come down. Whether because she has her answer, no one would say.'

countries.name: the vale of the Wray
countries.topic: the bridge at Wrayford
countries.rumour: 'Down the south road, where the drove roads come down off the fells, there's Wrayford, on the Wray,' says {keeper}, and lowers their voice. 'The carters rose against the bridge toll there a few nights back, and the lord's riders hanged three of them off the gatehouse on the bridge, and they're hanging there yet. The reeve says they stay till the lord's captain comes. Drovers coming through say the whole town goes and stands under them, and nobody will say a word.'
countries.heard: Away in the south of the country lies Wrayford, the bridge-city on the Wray, where the lord's riders hanged three carters from the gatehouse on the bridge after a rising against the toll, and the reeve keeps them hanging until the lord's captain comes.
countries.skyline: a town at a bridge, far down where the drove roads come off the fells
countries.far: the lord's riders hanged three carters from the gatehouse on the bridge, and they hang there yet

after.talk: The south road's news of Wrayford has gone to one sentence, which the carters say with their eyes on the table: the captain came, and the rail is bare, and nobody will tell it twice the same.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, the bridge and the rail and the captain's verdict, and refills your cup before you have finished. 'The drovers coming through said it went quiet after,' {keeper} says at last. 'They said a town can go quiet in two ways, and would not tell me which.' {keeper} turns the cup a quarter-turn on the bar. 'Do not tell me which. I shall have to pour for both kinds.'

countries.name: Calamy
countries.topic: the city of paper at the mouth of the Calam
countries.rumour: 'Away in the east of the country, where the cold country comes down to the sea and the river runs out through miles of reeds, there is Calamy, at the mouth of the Calam,' says {keeper}. 'A city of paper: tide-mills and binders and printers, and every house there keeps a book that knows it. They say the books have started to talk. And they burn their old almanacks at the Kindling, which is near, and this year nobody can say whether they ought.'
countries.heard: Away in the east of the country lies Calamy, at the mouth of the Calam, where every house keeps a book that knows it, and the books have begun to talk, and the Kindling is near.
countries.skyline: the sails of tide-mills turning along a coast of reeds
countries.far: the books of a city of paper have begun to talk, and the Kindling is near

after.talk: A barge-man up from the east says Calamy has had its Kindling, and that the books were in the room for it, and will say no more than that he did not stop to see.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the Kindling, and the Bound, and the Quick Sewn, and listens as one listens to a language one half understands. 'Books,' {keeper} says. 'That talked.' {keeper} lifts the account-book from under the bar, a plain one, and puts it down again, and then, more gently, back in the drawer. 'I've been writing in that for twenty years,' {keeper} says. 'It has never once answered.' A pause. 'I should not like to find out it has been listening.'

ash.told: {keeper} hears you out about the Kindling and the almanacks and the year of ash, and gets up to put another log on, which is not necessary. 'Three thousand,' {keeper} says. 'On a fire. After they had learned to speak.' {keeper} stands with the poker in one hand. 'I burned my father's letters when he died, and I have not stopped being sorry,' {keeper} says. 'It never occurred to me to ask them first.'

countries.name: the vale of the Arle
countries.topic: the Trial of the Wheel at Pentrice
countries.rumour: 'Away in the west of the country, where the Ise falls into the Arle, there's Pentrice,' says {keeper}. 'A minster town, very grand, where they license every word said on a stage and fine you for the rest. This week it's their Trial of the Wheel: three companies of players, three nights in a round playhouse over the river, and the best of them given a house of its own for ever.' {keeper} grins. 'They say old Absalom Gosse is going back for it, after forty years. They banned him from every stage inside the walls the last time. He started a riot.'
countries.skyline: a minster tower over a river town, where one river falls into another
countries.far: a minster town licenses every word said on a stage, and holds its Trial of the Wheel
countries.heard: Away in the west of the country lies Pentrice, a minster town that licenses every word said on a stage; this week it holds its Trial of the Wheel, three companies of players for three nights, and Absalom Gosse's company is going back after forty years' banishment.

notice.name: a playbill of the Trial of the Wheel
notice.text: A bill in red and black, much handled and rained on: THE TRIAL OF THE WHEEL AT PENTRICE. THREE COMPANIES OF PLAYERS. THREE NIGHTS. THE PATENT OF THE WHEEL TO BE GIVEN BY THE BENCH. BY LEAVE OF THE OFFICE OF PLAIN SPEECH. Under it someone has written in pencil: west road, a day; and drawn a bear.
notice.talk: A playbill of the Trial of the Wheel at Pentrice is nailed up where travellers will see it, and half the talk is of who will win the Patent and the other half of whether old Gosse will be let play at all.

after.talk: A playbill of the Trial of the Wheel at Pentrice still hangs where travellers will see it, curling at the corners. The Trial is over: the word off the west road is all of what happened on the last night, and nobody tells it the same way twice.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, all of it, from the Westgate to the verdict, and laughs in the right places, and once does not laugh at all. 'We heard some of it,' {keeper} says then. 'Off the west road. Not the half of it.' {keeper} reaches up and takes down the playbill of the Trial of the Wheel, and folds it, and puts it behind the bar, not on the fire.

countries.name: Pellam on the Lisk
countries.topic: the Frost Fair at Pellam
countries.rumour: 'West, up the country, where the North Road comes down to the Lisk, there's Pellam, the wool city,' says {keeper}. 'The river's frozen there for the first time in thirty-one winters, they say, bank to bank, and they're holding a Frost Fair on it: booths and a gin-tent and an ox roasting on the ice. And the ice has its own law while it lasts. A lie's no crime on it, and a handshake's the Court's.' {keeper} laughs. 'Half the rogues in the country will be there by now. The other half are on the way.'
countries.heard: Away in the west of the country lies Pellam on the Lisk, a wool city whose river has frozen for the first time in thirty-one winters; they are holding a Frost Fair on the ice, under the ice's own law: a lie is no crime on it, and a handshake is the Court's.
countries.skyline: a city on a river white with ice from bank to bank
countries.far: a river has frozen bank to bank under a wool city, and they hold a fair on it where a lie is no crime and a handshake is the law

countries.name: the Lim valley
countries.topic: the Season at Hessel
countries.rumour: 'Up in the north of the country, down in the Lim valley, there's Hessel,' says {keeper}, 'where the water comes up out of the hill hot, and the old go to be mended and the young to be married. It's the end of their Season. They say there's a rich old woman there who cooked for the navvies, buying husbands for all her family before she dies, and a house in the best street that's kept its shutters closed nine years, with the fires lit, in the warm.'
countries.heard: Up in the north of the country lies Hessel in the Lim valley, a spa where the water comes up hot and the old go to be mended and the young to be married; its Season is ending, a rich old woman there is buying husbands for her family before she dies, and a house in its best street has kept its shutters closed nine years.
countries.skyline: steam going up out of a green valley, where the water comes up out of the hill hot
countries.far: the water comes up out of a hill hot, and the old go there to be mended and the young to be married

countries.name: the Levels of Gaunt
countries.topic: the fell road to Gaunt
countries.rumour: 'Up in the north of the country the fell road goes up over Carth Fell and down to Gaunt,' says {keeper}, 'the city of the Minster, on the Levels, where they'll sell you somebody else's penance by the day. There's a heretic to be tried there on Ash Day, a barefoot man who used to do penance for half the Guildhall. They say a beadle went down the march road to fetch him, and has not come back up it.'
countries.heard: Up in the north of the country the fell road climbs over Carth Fell and comes down to Gaunt, a walled city on the Levels where penance is bought and sold by the day, and a barefoot heretic is to be tried on Ash Day.
countries.skyline: a walled city on a white plain, with a great church in it that has one tower and the stump of another
countries.far: penance is bought and sold by the day, and a barefoot heretic is to be tried at the Minster on Ash Day

after.talk: The fell road's news of Gaunt has gone quiet since Ash Day. A beadle has come back down the march road after all, without his man, and will not say where he left him.
after.told: {keeper} listens to the whole of it, the barefoot man and the Consistory and the Gate of Ash, and does not interrupt even at the penance by the day. 'Ash Day came and went up there,' {keeper} says. 'A beadle came down the road a week after, without his man, and sat where you are sitting, and asked for water, and then asked what Lent it was.' {keeper} sets down the cloth. 'I did not know how to answer him. I am not sure I know how to answer you.'

countries.name: the Gannet Reach
countries.topic: the wreck on the Gannet Reach
countries.rumour: 'North, up the country, the coast road goes down to the Gannet Reach,' says {keeper}, 'where the sea goes out twice a day and leaves nine miles of sand. There's a town on it called Skeel that lives off wrecks, and a big ship went onto the sands there a few nights back in fair weather, which ships don't. They're stripping her now. The Wreck Court sits on her in two days, and if nothing came ashore of her alive, she's theirs. They say there's a dog.'
countries.heard: Up in the north of the country the coast road goes down to the Gannet Reach, a tidal sea of sands and islands where the wrecking town of Skeel is stripping a merchantman that went onto the sands in fair weather; its Wreck Court sits in two days, and she is the town's only if nothing came ashore of her alive.
countries.skyline: a great flat shining to the west, sand or sea, with islands standing in it and a tower on one of them
countries.far: a ship went onto the sands of a tidal reach in fair weather, and the wrecking town there will have her if nothing came ashore alive

after.talk: Nobody talks of the Gannet Reach this week except to say the Wreck Court has sat on the ship in Skeel, and nobody quite agrees how it went.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about Skeel and the Court and the dog, and shakes their head slowly. 'A town that prays for wrecks,' {keeper} says. 'And it got one, and then it got you.' Whatever {keeper} thinks of that is kept for later.

countries.name: the Wold of Hume
countries.topic: the Wold of Hume, and its bees
countries.rumour: 'South, up on the Wold of Hume, past the mountains, there's a town lives inside a honeycomb under a cliff,' says {keeper}. 'Bees as big as hounds, and they'll sting a stranger dead unless he smells right. The candles come from there, the ones that burn three nights. And the word down the drove road is that their old queen's going to swarm, and half the town will walk off after her and never come back. They want hands to help them look for where.'
countries.heard: Away in the south of the country, past the mountains, lies the Wold of Hume, where a town lives inside a honeycomb under a cliff among bees as big as hounds; their old queen is about to swarm, half the town will walk after her, and their Searchers want hands to find where.
countries.skyline: a long grey brow of rock on the hills, and under it a glow like a lamp behind a curtain
countries.far: a town lives inside a honeycomb under a cliff, and half of it is about to walk away after a swarm

after.talk: The word down the drove road is that the bees on the Wold of Hume have swarmed, and half the town under the Brow walked off after them, and nobody yet knows where they have built.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the Wold, the Comb and the Leaving, and is quiet a while. 'Half of them,' {keeper} says at last. 'Just walked off. And the other half stood and watched them go.' {keeper} leans closer, then, and sniffs, and sits back with an odd look. 'You smell of honey,' {keeper} says. 'Did you know that? Like a summer field. It's in your clothes.'

countries.name: the Lull
countries.topic: the Lull, in the north of the country
countries.rumour: 'Up in the north of the country there's a hamlet called Sixways,' says {keeper}, 'and above it a stone, and past the stone a valley you can only walk into one day in seven. The other six the road goes round a hill and back. The Lull, they call it. They don't work in there: whatever's done there without meaning it comes apart at sunset, bread and money and all. And if you sleep a night in it, you lose a week out here.'
countries.heard: Up in the north of the country, above the hamlet of Sixways, a road goes down from a standing stone one day in seven into the Lull, a valley where whatever is done without meaning it comes apart at sunset, and a night slept is a week gone outside.
countries.skyline: a bare green hill with a standing stone on it, and a road that goes round the hill and comes back
countries.far: there is a valley you can only walk into one day in seven, where nothing done without meaning it lasts the day

after.talk: The talk from the north of the country is that something has changed in the Lull, and the carters of Sixways cannot agree whether for better.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the Lull, the stone and the bridge and the Watching, and is quiet a while. 'One day in seven,' {keeper} says at last. 'I've often thought I could do with that.' Then, after a moment: 'Or maybe not. Maybe I'd mean too little of it.'

countries.name: Larum and the Pass
countries.topic: the quiet over the Larum Pass
countries.rumour: 'West, up the country, at the head of a long valley, there's a hamlet called Larum under a high pass,' says {keeper}. 'For nine hundred years, on a still day, you could hear the dead fighting up there in the snow: like a smithy the size of the sky, faint, all day, and stopping at dusk. Larum sold their ballads. Forty days ago it stopped. The carters say Larum can't sleep for the quiet.'
countries.heard: Away in the west of the country, at the head of a long valley, lies Larum, under a high pass where for nine hundred years the warrior dead could be heard fighting in the snow, and stopped forty days ago; the carters say Larum cannot sleep for the quiet.
countries.skyline: a high pass full of a white cloud that never moves, between two shoulders of black rock
countries.far: the dead who fought every day in the snow above a mountain hamlet have stopped, and nobody knows why

after.talk: The carters coming down from the west say there is news out of Larum, and cannot agree whether the dead up the Pass have started again or not, and argue about it at the tables.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about Larum and the Pass and the town of shields, and is quiet a while. 'The dead,' {keeper} says at last. 'Making bread.' {keeper} shakes their head. 'My grandfather fought at Coldharbour. He always said he hoped there was nothing after. I'll not tell him.' Then, after a moment, looking at your hands: 'You're cold. Come to the fire.'

loud.told: {keeper} hears you out about Larum and the Pass and the town of shields, and is quiet a while. 'The carters said the sky up there had started again,' {keeper} says at last. 'Like a smithy, all day, on a still day. I thought they were drunk.' {keeper} shakes their head. 'The dead. Making bread, and going up in the morning to be killed again.' Then, after a moment, looking at your hands: 'You're cold. Come to the fire.'

countries.name: the Hollins country
countries.topic: the house on the hill at Hollins, over the march
countries.rumour: 'Up in the north of the country, in the hills, there's a village called Bootscrape,' says {keeper}, 'built on a doorstep. A giant's doorstep: the house it belongs to is as big as a hill, and stood shut three hundred years. The giantess has come home to it, they say, to die, and her woman wants a ratcatcher. Two crowns a day.' {keeper} lowers their voice. 'The carters say there's more than rats in the walls.'
countries.heard: Up in the north of the country, in the hills, the village of Bootscrape is built on the doorstep of Hollins, a giant's house as big as a hill, shut three hundred years. The giantess has come home to die, and her companion is hiring a ratcatcher; the carters say there is more than rats in the walls.
countries.skyline: a grey hill with a roof on it, and windows in its side as tall as churches
countries.far: a giantess has come home to die in a house as big as a hill, and there are people living in its walls

notice.name: a notice from Hollins
notice.text: A notice in a clear, pinched hand, carried down by a carter and nailed up where travellers will see it: WANTED, A RATCATCHER, FOR HOLLINS, THE HOUSE BEING OVERRUN. TWO CROWNS THE DAY, AND TWOPENCE THE TAIL. APPLY AT THE MAT, BOOTSCRAPE, TEN UNTIL TWO. D. PYECROFT. Under it, in pencil, someone has written: north over the march, and mind the cat.
notice.talk: A notice from Hollins is nailed up where travellers will see it, wanting a ratcatcher at two crowns a day, and the talk is of how big the rats must be in a house that size.

after.talk: The notice from Hollins still hangs where travellers will see it, curling at the corners; the carters say the giantess at Bootscrape is dead, and nobody wants a ratcatcher there now.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about Hollins: the Slot, the Wainscot, the Lady and her chart. 'People living in a giant's walls,' {keeper} says at last. 'And she never knew.' A pause. 'Or did she, by the end?' You tell them. {keeper} takes the notice down from the wall, and folds it, and puts it in a drawer instead of the fire.

countries.name: Sennet
countries.topic: the Grand Tour at Sennet
countries.rumour: 'Away in the east of the country, down on the coast, there's Sennet,' says {keeper}. 'A port, all glass-houses, with a House of Doors on the headland whose doors open on the planes, and a hill floating over the bay with the gentry living on it, and the merfolk living in the drowned streets underneath.' {keeper} leans on the bar. 'The Rector there has proclaimed a Grand Tour, the first in two hundred years. Whoever brings her the four petals of the Rose goes first through the Door of Doors, that opens on anywhere.' {keeper} lowers their voice. 'And a young lord went off the edge of the floating hill the night she proclaimed it, they say, in the fog.'
countries.heard: Away in the east of the country, down on the coast, lies Sennet: a port with a House of Doors whose doors open on the planes, a hill floating over its bay with the gentry on it, and merfolk in the drowned streets beneath. Its Rector has proclaimed a Grand Tour for the four petals of the Rose; the prize is to be first through the Door of Doors.
countries.skyline: far off over the sea, a hill hanging in the sky with houses on it, and a chain coming down from it
countries.far: a hill of houses floats over a bay, and the Rector of its House of Doors has proclaimed a Grand Tour

notice.name: the Rector's proclamation of the Grand Tour
notice.text: A printed sheet in four colours under a seal of a door: BY THE RECTOR OF THE HOUSE OF DOORS AT SENNET. THE GRAND TOUR IS PROCLAIMED, THE FIRST IN TWO HUNDRED YEARS. WHOSOEVER BRINGS TO THE HOUSE THE FOUR PETALS OF THE ROSE OF THE WINDS SHALL GO FIRST THROUGH THE DOOR OF DOORS. I. QUANCE, RECTOR. Under it, in pencil: east, down the coast road; and someone has drawn a little door, and beside it a little figure falling out of the sky.
notice.talk: The Rector of Sennet's proclamation of the Grand Tour is nailed up where travellers will see it, and half the talk is of the Door of Doors and what anybody would want with anywhere, and the other half of the young lord who fell out of the sky.

after.talk: The proclamation of the Grand Tour at Sennet still hangs where travellers will see it, curling at the corners. The word up the coast road is that the Tour is settled, one way or another, and nobody tells it the same way twice.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, all of it, from the coast road to the Door of Doors, and once, at the part about the hill, puts down the glass. 'We heard some of it,' {keeper} says then. 'Up the coast road. Not the half.' {keeper} takes the proclamation down, and folds it in four, and puts it behind the bar with the things worth keeping.

countries.name: Quittance
countries.topic: the Assured City of Quittance
countries.rumour: 'Up the north road there is Quittance,' says {keeper}. 'A river-port, eighty thousand souls, burned to the ground in my grandmother's time and built again on credit. Every house wears a plate over the door to say which Office will put it out. The brigades argue about whose door it is while it burns. They say the thing under the Exchange has not been paid, and that this year's Receipt is blank. The Offices take adjusters on, if you can add. I should insure your hat before you go in.'
countries.heard: Up the north road lies Quittance, a river-port that burned once and was rebuilt on credit, where every house wears the mark of the Office that will save it; and Reckoning is near, and the Receipt is said to be blank.
countries.skyline: smoke from a hundred chimneys, and not one of them rising straight
countries.far: a city insured house by house sits on something that has not been paid, and Reckoning is near

after.talk: There is a plate over the inn door now, a little crooked, that was not there before, and the landlord will not say what it is for. They say Quittance has come through its Reckoning, one way or another; the travellers who come down the north road have stopped asking after their hats.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out with a cloth in one hand and a pot in the other, and the pot does not move for a long time. 'Well,' {keeper} says at last. 'I always said it was a lot to put on one bell.' And sets the pot down, and pours you the first, and will not take your coin.

countries.name: Ombra
countries.topic: the Drawing at Ombra
countries.rumour: 'Away in the west, down in the delta where the river can't make up its mind, there is Ombra,' says {keeper}. 'It rains nine days in ten. By day nobody there is anybody; they go masked, bakers and ferrywomen and the Warden of Locks, and it is a hanging crime to say aloud who is under one.' {keeper} wipes a cup. 'Their Registrar's dead. The one who keeps the book of who is who. And there's a Drawing on the ninth night that has to be read by somebody, or every Office in the city runs out at midnight. They've sent for a stranger. It has to be a stranger.'
countries.heard: Away in the west, down in the delta, lies Ombra, a rainy city where everyone goes masked by day and it is a crime to say who is under a mask. Its Registrar is dead and the book of faces is gone, and unless somebody holds the Drawing on the ninth night, every Office in the city dissolves at midnight. The Watch has hired a stranger to look.
countries.skyline: far off to the west, low on the water under a lid of cloud, a city of grey roofs where every window has a lamp in it by day
countries.far: a rainy delta city goes masked by day, and its Registrar has died with the book of faces missing, nine days before the Drawing

notice.name: the Watch's notice from Ombra
notice.text: A square of grey paper stamped with a bare white oval, nailed up where travellers will see it: THE MASKED WATCH OF OMBRA WILL HIRE ONE STRANGER UNDER THE SEVENTY-FIRST ARTICLE OF THE CONCORD. NO NAME, NO MASK, NO STANDING REQUIRED. APPLY AT THE GATE OF STRANGERS ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE NOVENA, AT THE THIRD BELL. The bottom has been torn off, and in pencil, in a different hand: Nine days. It is always raining.
notice.talk: The Watch of Ombra's notice is nailed up where travellers will see it, and half the talk is of the city that goes masked by day and what a Registrar is, and the other half of why they would need a stranger.

after.talk: The Watch of Ombra's notice still hangs where travellers will see it, curling in the damp. The word down the west road is that the Drawing was held, one way or another, and that nobody tells it the same way twice.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out, all of it, from the Gate of Strangers to the Urn Hall, and at the part about the name said kindly puts down the cup. 'We heard some of it,' {keeper} says then. 'Down the west road. Not the half.' {keeper} takes the Watch's notice off its nail, and smooths it flat with the side of a hand, and puts it away behind the bar with the things worth keeping.

countries.name: Tolleth and the Skerrow passage
countries.topic: the sailing to Skerrow out of Tolleth
countries.rumour: 'Down the coast, at Tolleth, there's a ketch called the Dorothea,' says {keeper}, 'that sails for an island nobody goes to. Skerrow. A night and a morning out, past a reef they call the Combs. There's a lamp on it, older than the roads. The captain's short of hands, and short of money, and sails on the noon ebb whether you're aboard or no.'
countries.heard: Down the coast at Tolleth the ketch Dorothea sails on the noon ebb for Skerrow, an island a night and a morning out past a reef called the Combs, where a lamp has burned since before the roads.
countries.skyline: masts, close as reeds, in a harbour the colour of slate
countries.far: a ketch sails from a slate-grey harbour to an island with a lamp older than the roads

after.talk: Tolleth's board has the Dorothea's sailings in chalk again, and the talk down the coast is of Skerrow and what the lamp is doing, now that somebody has been out to see.
after.told: {keeper} takes in all of it, the Combs and the lamp and the island that nobody goes to, and does not say anything for a full minute. 'The Dorothea has been in and out of Tolleth twice since she brought the news,' {keeper} says. 'Same hour. Always an hour earlier than anyone expects.' {keeper} nods at the window. 'You will have thought it a long way to go for a lamp. I never knew anyone who went for the lamp.'

countries.name: Tallow Edge
countries.topic: the pale ridge that swallows a river
countries.rumour: 'West of here there is a long white ridge called Tallow Edge,' says {keeper}, 'and a river that goes into it at one end and comes out the other. There was a mine in it once. The village at the foot of it, Swallet, will not talk of it, except Lowen Pook at the Chandler's Arms, who will tell you the half she can bear. There is a smugglers' road underneath, they say, and something older than that.'
countries.heard: West of here lies Tallow Edge, a long pale ridge that swallows a river, with an abandoned mine in it, a smugglers' road under it, and something older than either.
countries.skyline: a long bare ridge, white as tallow, with a thread of mist coming out of its foot
countries.far: a river goes in at one end of a white ridge and comes out the other, and nobody in the village will talk about what is between

after.talk: There is talk along the carters' road of a village under a white ridge that has put a page up on a beam. Nobody can say what is on it. A drover swears the brandy that came through the ridge last year does not come through any more.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the ridge and the dead and the hill under the hill, and takes the names from you one at a time, as you give them, saying each over under {keeper}'s breath. 'Fourteen,' {keeper} says at the end. 'My mother's cousin was in the Company's shaft the winter they broke the wall. We were told Porthwen. We were told he had gone for work.' {keeper} writes something on the back of a bill and puts it in a drawer with the keys. 'I'll not say anything to her,' {keeper} says. 'But I'll go and look at that page myself, in spring.'

road.told: {keeper} hears you out about the white ridge and the road under it, and laughs aloud at the end of it, once, in disbelief. 'Two miles of Aenean pavement under the hill the excise never walked,' {keeper} says. 'There's a toll-house on the downs that will want to know about that. Then again, there isn't, is there? Not now.' {keeper} turns the matter over. 'You've been very free,' {keeper} says, 'with other people's secrets.' And then, because you look it: 'Sit down. I only mean it as an observation.'

countries.name: the Hesper Fells
countries.topic: the old road over the Hesper Fells
countries.rumour: 'East of here, up in the Hesper Fells, there is a village called Kell Ford,' says {keeper}, 'where a paved road begins that nobody has finished walking, and a reeve, Greta Hennick, who keeps the road-book and will let you read it. The soldiers built it. They say it goes sixty miles over the fells to a place where somebody still lights the lamps. Every spring somebody in Kell puts a lamp in the window, and nobody will say for whom.'
countries.heard: East of here, in the Hesper Fells, lies Kell Ford, where an old soldiers' road begins that goes sixty miles over the mountains to a place where, they say, someone still lights the lamps.
countries.skyline: a pale paved road climbing out of a huddle of grey houses into the fells and being lost
countries.far: an old soldiers road goes sixty miles over the fells, and at the far end someone is said to still light the lamps

after.talk: The talk from the fells this season is of the paved road, and of whether the lamps at the far end are still lit, and of a reeve called Hennick who has had something to say about it to everyone who passes. Nobody has said what.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the road and the Cohort and what was said in the forum, and for a while does not speak. 'Sixty miles,' {keeper} says, 'and every mile paved by somebody who thought it would be walked.' {keeper} stands, and goes to the window, and looks out at the road that goes east, which is not paved. 'Do you know,' {keeper} says, 'I have never once asked where it went.' And then, without turning: 'I think I will light the lamp tonight. You needn't tell me for whom.'

countries.name: the Aldwater
countries.topic: the Staithe quay, where two barges lie side by side
countries.rumour: 'Down at Staithe quay,' says {keeper}, 'they keep two barges side by side that no one can tell apart, the Maud and the Mary. A person once got on the wrong one, and the river has never forgiven him.'
countries.heard: South of here, at the Staithe quay on the Aldwater, two barges lie side by side that nobody can tell apart.
countries.skyline: a brown river between willows with a line of masts on it
countries.far: two barges that nobody can tell apart lie side by side on a river, and one of them is the wrong one

after.talk: The barges are still side by side at the Staithe, they say, and still alike. What has changed is that nobody on the quay will now say which is which, and they say it with some pride.
after.told: {keeper} laughs before you have finished, and then stops, and asks you to go back to the part about the box. 'The Maud and the Mary,' {keeper} says, shaking a head. 'A woman off a boat last month swore the Maud had never been so heavy. Another swore it was the Mary that sank.' {keeper} leans across. 'They are both afloat. I have it from a man who has sat on both.'

countries.name: Scarth Holm
countries.topic: the lighthouse at the end of the Scarth causeway
countries.rumour: 'There is a light at the end of the Scarth sands,' says {keeper}, 'and a causeway that dries for three hours at noon, and a keeper called Seddon who has never once turned a traveller from his kitchen door. Cross after twelve and you sleep out there. People do, and are glad of the tea, and do not much talk of the night.'
countries.heard: East of here, a lighthouse stands on a rock at the end of a tidal causeway, and the road to it is only dry for three hours.
countries.skyline: a white tower on a grey flat, with posts going out to it
countries.far: a lighthouse stands at the end of a causeway that the sea closes every day, and people who cross late stay the night

after.talk: The coast road has stopped telling people to cross before twelve. It has not started saying why. A carter who has been out to the Scarth light says only that the tea is as good as ever, and puts his hand flat on the table.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the light and the sands and the cistern, and does not say a word until you have finished. Then {keeper} gets up and puts the shutters across the window on the sea side, which was not what you expected, and comes back. 'My father used to say the Scarth keepers were the only men in the county who slept with their boots on,' {keeper} says. 'I took it for a joke.' Then, quietly: 'Was there tea?' You say there was. 'Good,' says {keeper}. 'That's something.'

dark.told: {keeper} hears you out about the light and the sands and the cistern, and sits for a while with both hands round a cup that has gone cold. 'A keeper gone,' {keeper} says, 'or someone who came for the dead. It is a hard rock.' {keeper} looks at the shutter, the one on the sea side. 'They'll not leave the lamp dark. They never do. Somebody walks out at noon with a can of oil and a face like yours.' Then, getting up: 'I'll find you a bed that faces inland.'

countries.name: the vale of the Brimble
countries.topic: the ford at Sallowfield, where a coach has cracked its axle
countries.rumour: 'There's a village on the Brimble called Sallowfield,' says {keeper}, 'a ford, a mill, sixty souls, and Nan Ashworth at the Ploughshare, who gives a bed to anyone and an opinion to everyone. A coach broke its axle there this week, and I'm told there's a company of the Margrave's unpaid soldiers coming down the east road behind it with nothing in their bellies. Whoever's passing would do well to be passing quickly.' {keeper} wipes a mug. 'The smith will tell you three days for the axle. I'd say the soldiers will be quicker.'
countries.heard: West of here, on the Brimble, lies Sallowfield: a ford, a mill, sixty people, and a coach with a cracked axle, with a company of the Margrave's unpaid soldiers coming down the east road behind it.
countries.skyline: a river valley with a mill-race and a chapel tower, and smoke going straight up from every chimney
countries.far: a village at a ford is waiting, and nobody in it knows yet what to do about the soldiers on the road

after.talk: The talk this week is of Sallowfield on the Brimble, and of the Margrave's unpaid company, and of which of the two is still standing. Nobody here has been there. Everyone has a cousin who has.
after.told: {keeper} hears you out about the ford and the green and the three nights, and does not interrupt, which for {keeper} is a kind of tribute. 'Sixty souls,' {keeper} says at the end, 'and a coach.' {keeper} turns the mug on the bar. 'The coach went on, I suppose. They always do.' And then, setting it down: 'Nan Ashworth sent me a letter at Michaelmas, last year, about a cheese. I've never answered it. I think I'll answer it.'

burned.told: {keeper} hears you out about the ford and the three nights and the green, and goes quiet at the word green. 'Black timbers,' {keeper} says. 'And the chapel standing.' {keeper} looks for a long time at nothing. 'Nan Ashworth had a cellar she said had never in its life been lent to an army,' {keeper} says. 'I hope that is still true. I should like it to be the last true thing.' {keeper} pours, and does not put the price on the slate.
